concurrent.3: Concurrent Processing Concurrent processing is a computing model in which multiple processors execute instructions simultaneously for better performance. Concurrent means, which occurs when something else happens.
concurrent.4: Multiprogramming Environment In a multiprogramming environment, there are multiple tasks shared by one processor.
concurrent.5: Multiprocessing Environment In multiprocessing environment two or more processors are used with shared memory.
concurrent.6: Better Performance When one application only utilizes the processor, and another only uses the disk drive, the time it takes to perform both apps simultaneously is less than the time it takes to run them sequentially. Better Resource Utilization It enables resources that are not being used by one application to be used by another. Running Multiple Applications It enables you to execute multiple applications simultaneously. Advantages
concurrent.7: It is necessary to protect multiple applications from each other. It is necessary to use extra techniques to coordinate several applications. Additional performance overheads and complexities in OS are needed for switching between applications. Disadvantages
concurrent.8: separate applications running on one system Fully independent Independent but related separate applications running on one system but its functionalities are interconnected to other processes Relationship between processes
concurrent.9: Scenario C: The Shared Printer You and your classmate both hit “Print”; at the same time. You are printing a 10-page essay, and they are printing a 15-page report.
concurrent.10: Q5: Why must the printer finish one print job before starting another? The printer can only be used by one job at a time. If it printed the 10-page essay and the 15-page report at the same time, the pages from both documents would get mixed together, and both outputs would be useless. To prevent this, the OS gives the printer to one job at a time and puts other jobs in a queue until the current one finishes. This is an example of mutual exclusion.
concurrent.11: Mutual Exclusive It is necessary for some resources to remain allocated to a process for as long as process requires. Serial reusable resources require mutual exclusion. Example: The printer is being used by a process then it must remain allocated to the process until printout is complete.
concurrent.12: Mutual exclusion gives rise to another problem which OS must handle – deadlock.
concurrent.13: Scenario A: The Group Project Standoff Two students, Alice and Bob, are working on a project in the library. There is only ONE Reference Book and ONE shared Calculator on the table. ● Alice grabs the Reference Book. She reads it and realizes she now needs the Calculator to finish her math, but she refuses to let go of the book until her task is 100% complete. ● At the exact same time, Bob grabs the Calculator. He does some math, but realizes he now needs the Reference Book to finish his formula. He refuses to let go of the Calculator until his task is 100% complete.
concurrent.14: Q1: What happens to Alice and Bob's progress? Will either of them ever finish their task? Neither Alice nor Bob can make any more progress. Alice is holding one resource and waiting for the one Bob has, while Bob is holding the other resource and waiting for the one Alice has. Since neither will let go of what they are holding, they will wait forever and neither will finish their task. This situation is called a deadlock.
concurrent.15: Q2: What rule would you invent to resolve this standoff? I would make a rule that everyone must request resources in the same fixed order. For example, every student must get the Reference Book first before they can get the Calculator. This way, no one can hold the Calculator while waiting for the Book, so the circular waiting between Alice and Bob can never happen. Another possible rule is that a student must get all the resources they need at once, or release everything they are holding if they cannot get the rest.
concurrent.16: Deadlock Deadlock is where a process is waiting for an event that will never occur. Example: Process P1 has a printer allocated and is attempting to open a file F. Process P2 has already obtained exclusive access to file F and now requests printer. Each process is waiting for a resource held by the other, while holding a resource required by the other.
concurrent.19: Busy Waiting The area of a process which is sensitive to inter-process complications is called the critical region. To guarantee mutual exclusion only one process is allowed to enter its critical region at a time.
concurrent.21: Scenario B: The Last Airline Ticket There is exactly ONE seat left on a flight to Palawan. Agent X (in Manila) and Agent Y (in Cebu) both look at the system and see “1 Seat Available”. They both click “Book” for their respective clients at the exact same millisecond.
concurrent.22: Q3: What disastrous real-world result happens if the system cannot coordinate them? Both agents could see the last seat as available and book it at the same time for two different passengers. This results in double-booking, where two people pay for the same seat but only one can actually use it. This happens because both agents read the seat's status before either of them finished updating it, which is an example of a race condition.
concurrent.23: Q4: Should the system lock the entire database or only the specific flight/seat? Explain. The system should lock only the specific seat (record) being booked. Locking the entire database would block everyone else from booking any other flight, even ones that have nothing to do with this seat, which would make the system very slow. Locking just the seat protects it from double-booking while still letting other customers book other seats and flights at the same time.
concurrent.25: File and record locking Mutual exclusion is required in file processing where several users are accessing the same file (databases) Example: airline booking system, one seat left two agents access at same time before file is updated and seat is double booked. Solution is file locking, preventing access to the file while it is being updated
concurrent.26: File lock Whole file is locked, prevents any other process accessing any part of that file. Write lock if a specific set of data is write locked, it prevents other process modifying or reading data Read lock Set of data is read locked other processes may read data but no process can modify it. files.5: 04 Definition A file is a named collection of related information that is recorded on secondary storage such as magnetic disks, magnetic tapes and optical disks. In general, a file is a sequence of bits, bytes, lines or records whose meaning is defined by the files creator and user. CIT.015 OPERATING SYSTEMS
files.6: 05 File Structure A file has a certain defined structure according to its type. A text file is a sequence of characters organized into lines. A source file is a sequence of procedures and functions. An object file is a sequence of bytes organized into blocks that are understandable by the machine. When operating system defines different file structures, it also contains the code to support these file structure. Unix, MS-DOS support minimum number of file structure. CIT.015 OPERATING SYSTEMS A File Structure should be according to a required format that the operating system can understand.
files.8: 07 File System File systems are a crucial part of any operating system, providing a structured way to store, organize and manage data on storage devices such as hard drives, SSDs and USB drives. FAT, NTFS, ext, HFS, APFS CIT.015 OPERATING SYSTEMS
files.9: 07 File System User Application: The programs or software that request file operations like read, write, or delete. Logical File System: Manages metadata, file names, directories, and access permissions. Virtual File System (VFS): Acts as a bridge, allowing different file systems to work under a single interface. Physical File System: Handles the actual storage of data blocks on the disk. Partition 1, Partition 2, Partition 3: Divisions of the storage device where files are stored physically. CIT.015 OPERATING SYSTEMS

files.11: 07 File Type File type refers to the ability of the operating system to distinguish different types of file such as text files source files and binary files etc. Many operating systems support many types of files. CIT.015 OPERATING SYSTEMS
files.12: 08 Ordinary Files These are the files that contain user information. These may have text, databases or executable program. The user can apply various operations on such files like add, modify, delete or even remove the entire file. CIT.015 OPERATING SYSTEMS
files.13: 09 Directory Files These files contain list of file names and other information related to these files. CIT.015 OPERATING SYSTEMS
files.14: 10 Special Files These files are also known as device files. These files represent physical device like disks, terminals, printers, networks, tape drive etc. CIT.015 OPERATING SYSTEMS
files.15: 11 File Access Mechanisms Sequential Access A sequential access is that in which the records are accessed in some sequence, i.e., the information in the file is processed in order, one record after the other. Indexed sequential access This mechanism is built up on base of sequential access. An index is created for each file which contains pointers to various blocks. Index is searched sequentially and its pointer is used to access the file directly. Direct/Random access Random access file organization provides, accessing the records directly. Each record has its own address on the file with by the help of which it can be directly accessed for reading or writing. The records need not be in any sequence within the file and they need not be in adjacent locations on the storage medium. CIT.051 OPERATING SYSTEM
files.17: 13 Space Allocation Contiguous Allocation Each file occupies a contiguous address space on disk. Assigned disk address is in linear order. Easy to implement. External fragmentation is a major issue with this type of allocation technique. Indexed Allocation Provides solutions to problems of contiguous and linked allocation. A index block is created having all pointers to files. Each file has its own index block which stores the addresses of disk space occupied by the file. Directory contains the addresses of index blocks of files. Linked Allocation Each file carries a list of links to disk blocks. Directory contains link / pointer to first block of a file. No external fragmentation Effectively used in sequential access file. Inefficient in case of direct access file. CIT.015 OPERATING SYSTEM
